title: How To Not Get Annoyed When Your Students Misbehave
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that visibly getting annoyed at student misbehavior — even without a word spoken, through sighs and body language — invites more misbehavior, because students target emotionally weakened teachers. He describes the escalation pattern: once students sense they've gotten under a teacher's skin, they challenge authority more, lie when caught, and even recruit otherwise well-behaved peers into testing the teacher further. His solution is to shift the entire emotional burden of misbehavior off the teacher and onto the classroom management plan itself, so the teacher becomes merely a neutral 'referee' enforcing a pre-taught, impersonal system rather than a party to any conflict. He frames this as freeing rather than harsh: once a teacher proves they aren't emotionally invested and won't argue, negotiate, or bargain, students' respect and appreciation grow, and the teacher is freed to focus on lessons, rapport, and enjoyment of the job.
points: Getting visibly annoyed at misbehavior — even silently through sighs and body language — signals weakness that invites more misbehavior.
Once students sense they can get under a teacher's skin, even normally well-behaved students may join in to impress peers.
Shift the entire emotional burden of misbehavior onto the classroom management plan itself; the teacher's job is only to teach it and follow it exactly.
Never argue, explain, bargain, or negotiate when enforcing a consequence — deliver it and move on, like a referee calling a foul.
Proving you're merely the neutral enforcer of a promised system, not an emotionally invested party, is what ultimately builds students' respect and appreciation.
quotes: If you get annoyed when your students misbehave, then it’s going to lead to more misbehavior. Even if you don’t say a word.
Students prey upon emotionally weakened teachers like jackals on the hunt.
The most accurate sign that your students have gotten to you is when you try to hold them accountable and they lie to you.
It’s to remove all burden of misbehavior off of yourself and direct its weight fully and 100 percent onto your students.
The relationship between you and your classroom management plan is distant. In fact, you have very little to do with it. Once it’s taught, you just follow it.
Most of all, however, is that once you’ve proven that you’re just the messenger, defender exemplar, and one and only leader of the classroom, your students will become transformed.
